# Linear Regression 

Linear regression is one approach to modeling. It covers simple stuff (t tests) to complex stuff (automated variable selection via penalization) 

* observe data for subjects 1 to n. Want to estimate Beta... in the model 

* assumptions, residuals have mean zero, constant variance, and are independent 

* estimate parameters using OLS 

Predictors 
Outcome is continuous, predictors can be anything
categorical predictors require indicator variables (for each non-reference group, a binary variable indicating group membership for each subject is created and used in the model) 

Testing 
For a single regression coefficient, you can construct a test statistic 

For large samples this has a standard normal distribution 

Diagnostics 
Many model assumptions can be examinded using residuals 

* look at overall distribution 
* look at residuals vs predictors 

Generalized linear models 
* appropriate for non-continuous

Linear models in R 
`lm` for linear models 
`glm` for generalized linear models 

output is complex, use `broom` package to clean up 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)

set.seed(1)
```

```{r}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

options(
  ggplot2.continuous.colour = "viridis",
  ggplot2.continuous.fill = "viridis"
)

scale_colour_discrete = scale_colour_viridis_d
scale_fill_discrete = scale_fill_viridis_d
```

## Airbnb 

```{r}
data("nyc_airbnb")
```

```{r}
nyc_airbnb = 
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate(
    stars = review_scores_location / 2
  ) |> 
  rename(
    borough = neighbourhood_group, 
    neighborhood = neighbourhood 
  ) |> 
  filter(
    borough != "Staten Island"
  ) |> 
  select(price, stars, borough, neighborhood, room_type)
```

Fit a linear regression 

```{r}
fit = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb) #borough is indicator variable, bronx is reference category because it is first alphabetically 
```

Look at what we have 

```{r}
summary(fit)
coef(fit)
fitted.values(fit) #all 40,000 fitted values 
resid(fit) #computes all residuals 
names(fit) # what are names of stuff in fit? 
```

most of this output is bad, but sometimes it is okay 

let's do better. tidy it with broom!  

```{r}
broom::tidy(fit) |> #pulls out stuff you probably care about, formats it as df, works on almost everything 
  select(-std.error) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

broom::glance(fit) #quick information that is potentially relevant 
```

Change reference category 

```{r}
fit = 
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate(
    borough = fct_infreq(borough)
  ) |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = _)


broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  select(-std.error, -statistic) |> 
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")) |> # just constructing term variables in a nicer way to look at 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Diagnostics 

Basically looking at residuals 

```{r}
modelr::add_residuals(nyc_airbnb, fit) # which model are you adding residuals from? fit --> adds column to aibnb df with these residuals 
```

So we can look at residuals 

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = stars, y = resid)) +
  geom_point() #residual distribution - it is skewed! 

nyc_airbnb |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = borough, y = resid)) +
  geom_violin()
```

## Hypothesis testing 

```{r}
broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
We know this is skewed, so we would not trust this significance fully - do permutation testing in this situation (we won't talk about it in this class) 

Try testing nested models 

```{r}
fit_null = lm(price ~ stars, data = nyc_airbnb)
fit_alt = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)

anova(fit_null, fit_alt) #compares the two models
```

## Nesting data 

try a more complicated model 

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  lm(price ~ stars * borough + room_type * borough, data = _) |>  #do stars and borough have an interaction? does the effect of stars differ depending on which borough you are in? 
  broom::tidy() |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

stars : main effect of stars in reference category (bronx) 

What if I want to know what's happening in Manhattan?
```{r}
 nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy()

 nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Bronx") |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy()
```
Now we're back to iteration - I want to fit same model over and over 

Create a quick function
```{r}
airbnb_lm = function(data) {
  
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = data)
  
}
```

fit that function to each column we care about 
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |>  #nesting everything except borough - dfs that go with each borough in df
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm), 
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy) #tidying up results of column you just created (lm fits)
  ) |> 
  pull(results)
```

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |>  #nesting everything except borough - dfs that go with each borough in df
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm), 
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy) #tidying up results of column you just created (lm fits)
  ) |> 
  select(-datasets, -fits) |> 
  unnest(results) |> #fancy it up!
  select(borough, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term, 
    values_from = estimate
  )
```
Effect of stars is strongest in Manhattan and weakest in the Bronx. this does not answer "does stars matter in a stat sig way?" need to make alt model and do an F test for that. this is good for EDA though 

Creating anonymous function
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |>  #nesting everything except borough - dfs that go with each borough in df
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, \(data) lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = data)), #shorthand for creating same function, get same results as above
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy) #tidying up results of column you just created (lm fits)
  ) |> 
  select(-datasets, -fits) |> 
  unnest(results) |> #fancy it up!
  select(borough, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term, 
    values_from = estimate
  )
```


```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |> 
  nest(datasets = -neighborhood) |> 
  mutate( 
    fits = map(datasets, \(df) lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = df)), 
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
    ) |> 
  select(neighborhood, results) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  filter(term == "room_typePrivate room") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = neighborhood, y = estimate)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 80, hjust = 1))
```
The entire home/apartment will be much more expensive in some of these neighborhoods (-100 means you will save $100)
